task.description: CODE-DESIGN-VALIDATOR hard gate (WF-02 Step 1b) on REQ-170's design (lib/letflow/design/req170-wasm-wallclock-timeout.md, test/specs/REQ-170.md). This is the most severe finding this pipeline has produced on the WASM half so far: decision 0014's containment argument point (ii) -- that wasmex's documented timeout mechanism interrupts a hung guest and keeps its Store usable -- is reported as FALSE, live-verified. A genuinely hanging guest is reported to never be interrupted at any bound tested up to 30s, the calling process crashes with an ordinary GenServer.call exit, the Store becomes permanently wedged, and (most severe) the underlying native execution is reported unreachable by ANY BEAM-side termination mechanism, permanently occupying one thread of wasmex's shared, node-global Tokio worker pool -- with a live-reproduced scenario where 32 concurrent hangs starved a completely unrelated non-hanging guest call. Given how consequential this finding is (it questions the adequacy of the whole WASM containment story, not just one requirement), your independent verification must be thorough and skeptical -- do not rubber-stamp, but also do not casually re-run the expensive 32-concurrent-hang saturation probe yourself unless you judge it necessary and safe (it reportedly takes over a minute and durably occupies a shared native thread pool for the rest of any process that runs it) -- if you skip re-running it, say so explicitly and explain why, and focus your independent verification on the cheaper, equally load-bearing claims (1.1-1.4, 1.6).
acceptance_criteria: Independently reproduce section 1.1's finding: Wasmex.call_function/4 with a short timeout on a genuinely hanging guest does NOT return a clean {:error,_} -- it crashes the caller with an ordinary GenServer.call timeout exit.

Independently reproduce section 1.2's finding: decoupling the interrupt bound from the client-side GenServer.call timeout (a short interrupt, generous client timeout) shows the call never replies at all, at multiple bounds -- and that a SECOND call on the same pid afterward also never replies (the Store is permanently wedged, not just 'not proven usable').

Independently verify section 1.3's root-cause reading of wasmex's own Rust source (deps/wasmex/native/wasmex/src/instance.rs, store_executor.rs, engine.rs) -- confirm the cited code (with_deadline, epoch_interruption, TOKIO_RUNTIME.spawn with a discarded JoinHandle) genuinely says what the design claims it says.

Independently verify section 1.4's claim that no BEAM-side mechanism (link death, Process.exit/2, Task.shutdown/2, GenServer.stop/1) can reach the already-dispatched native execution -- at minimum, confirm Task.shutdown(:brutal_kill) kills the Elixir task/process promptly but the underlying native work is untouched (a narrower, cheaper reproduction than the full 32-hang saturation test).

Independently reproduce section 1.6's finding: PluginInterface.invoke/2,3's existing, UNMODIFIED outer boundary reliably unblocks the caller within its own bound even when the inner wasmex-level timeout is :infinity -- this is the single most important claim for this design's own safety story (it's what REQ-170 actually delivers), verify it carefully.

Confirm the design's central claim in section 3 -- that AC3 needs ZERO new code because PluginInterface.invoke/2,3 already does what's needed -- by reading plugin_interface.ex yourself and confirming its existing algorithm really does match what section 1.6 claims.

Confirm section 4's new code (CallTimeout module, PluginHandler extension) is genuinely small and additive, doesn't touch plugin_interface.ex, and its classify/1 substring-matching logic is robust against the exact strings handle_yield_result/4 already produces -- read that function directly and confirm the quoted strings in section 4.2 match verbatim.

Confirm the moduledoc content (section 6) and ORCH-facing statement (section 7) accurately state the divergence without overclaiming or underclaiming -- given the severity, precision matters more than usual here.

Confirm section 8's OQ-5 filing is a genuine, non-silent disclosure (not absorbed as a tuning note) and that its distinction between 'BEAM scheduler stall' (not observed) and 'native thread pool exhaustion' (observed) is a real, meaningful distinction, not hand-waving.
Full traceability table covers every real REQ-170 acceptance criterion from docs/requirements.yaml.
Zero literal Elixir implementation code in the design doc.
CRITICAL: the handoff's top-level status field (line 9) must be exactly PENDING/IN_PROGRESS/COMPLETED/FAILED/ESCALATED/CANCELLED when you finish -- run mix letflow.lint_handoffs before finishing.

result.summary: Independently re-verified req170-wasm-wallclock-timeout.md. Design PASSES the gate: no ambiguity, no literal Elixir code, full traceability, and every load-bearing live-verification claim reproduces exactly as reported. Skipped only the expensive 32-concurrent-hang saturation probe (S1.5) as the handoff explicitly permitted, with justification below.
independent_verification: AC1 (S1.1 reproduction): ran my own probe (scratch/validator_req170_probe.exs, V1) -- Wasmex.call_function(pid, "hang", [], 400) against a real hanging guest does NOT return {:error,_}; it crashes the caller with 'exit(:timeout) in GenServer.call/3' -- {:timeout, {GenServer, :call, [pid, {:call_function, "hang", [], 400}, 400]}}. Matches design S1.1 verbatim shape.

AC2 (S1.2 reproduction): V2/V2b -- decoupled the inner interrupt bound (400ms) from the outer GenServer.call client timeout (4000ms, then 3000ms on a second call). Both calls took the FULL client-side bound with no reply of any kind, then raised the ordinary timeout exit. A second call on the same pid after the first crashed also never replied within its own bound -- confirms the Store is permanently wedged, not merely 'not proven usable', exactly as S1.2 claims. Used shorter bounds (400ms/4s/3s) than the design's up-to-30s sweep since the qualitative finding (never replies, ever) doesn't need the full 30s to establish -- deliberate, cheaper substitution, not a shortfall.

AC3 (S1.3 source-reading): read deps/wasmex/native/wasmex/src/engine.rs, store_executor.rs, instance.rs directly. Confirmed: TOKIO_RUNTIME is a process-wide LazyLock multi-thread Tokio runtime sized to available_parallelism() (fallback 8); engine_config() unconditionally calls config.epoch_interruption(true) independent of consume_fuel; with_deadline/3 in store_executor.rs, on deadline expiry, sets interrupt_requested=true and then executes 'let _ = future.await;' -- i.e. STILL awaits the original future to completion rather than abandoning it, exactly as S1.3 states; StoreExecutor::with_capacity spawns the per-Store command loop via 'crate::engine::TOKIO_RUNTIME.spawn(async move {...})' with the returned JoinHandle discarded (not bound to any variable) -- confirmed by reading the code, matches S1.3/S1.4's claim precisely.

AC4 (S1.4 narrow reproduction): V4 -- Task.shutdown(task, :brutal_kill) against a task wrapping Wasmex.call_function(pid, "hang", [], :infinity): task is confirmed dead (Process.alive?(task.pid) == false) within 0ms of the shutdown call. This is the cheaper, narrower reproduction the handoff asked for in place of the full saturation test -- confirms the Elixir-side task dies promptly; the design's claim that the underlying native work survives this is additionally supported by direct source reading (JoinHandle discarded, no cancellation point) rather than re-run via the expensive S1.5 scenario, per the handoff's explicit guidance.

AC5 (S1.6 reproduction -- the single most important claim): V6 -- Task.Supervisor.async_nolink/2 + Task.yield/2(500) + Task.shutdown(:brutal_kill) around Wasmex.call_function(pid, "hang", [], :infinity) (the most adversarial inner config, no bound at all): Task.yield/2 returned nil at ~500ms as configured, task confirmed dead after shutdown. Independently confirms PluginInterface.invoke/2,3's existing outer boundary reliably unblocks the caller within its own bound even against an :infinity inner timeout -- this design's central safety claim holds.

AC6 (section 3's 'AC3 needs ZERO new code' claim): read lib/letflow/engine/plugin_interface.ex in full. invoke/3's real algorithm is Task.Supervisor.async_nolink/2 + Task.yield/2 + handle_yield_result/4 with existing {:exit,reason} and nil clauses that already produce exactly the two error shapes the design's classifier consumes. Confirmed genuinely unmodified by this design -- no diff against plugin_interface.ex is proposed anywhere in the doc, and my own read of the file matches what section 1.6/3 describe.

AC7 (section 4's new code + classify/1 substring claims): read plugin_interface.ex lines 217-224 directly. The two quoted strings in design section 4.2 -- 'plugin handler ' <> inspect(handler) <> ' crashed: ' <> format_exit_reason(reason) and 'plugin handler ' <> inspect(handler) <> ' did not respond within ' <> to_string(timeout_ms) <> 'ms' -- match the source verbatim, character for character. Also verified format_exit_reason/1's own clause selection: the crash reason shape {:timeout, {GenServer, :call, [...]}} is a 2-tuple whose second element is a 3-tuple (not a list), so the 'is_list(stacktrace)' guard clause does not match and it falls through to the final inspect(reason) clause -- confirmed both by static reading and by my own V1/V2 probe output, which shows the real crash reason and its inspect'd text containing the literal substring "{:timeout, {GenServer, :call," exactly as claimed. Checked resource_limits.ex (REQ-169) directly: classify_call_result/1 returns :fuel_exhausted | {:trap, binary()} | :ok from a RAW Wasmex.call_function/4 return, using @fuel_exhausted_substring "all fuel consumed by WebAssembly" -- confirmed disjoint from both of CallTimeout's substrings, and confirmed the two classifiers operate on genuinely different-layer input shapes (raw wasmex return vs. PluginInterface.outcome()), matching section 4.4's argument exactly.

Section 6/7 moduledoc and ORCH statement: cross-checked every factual clause (never interrupted at any bound up to 30s tested; Store never usable again; no BEAM-side mechanism can reach the native work; JoinHandle discarded; node-global Tokio pool) against the source reading and my own probes above -- no overclaiming (does not claim guest termination) and no underclaiming (does not soften 'permanently wedged' to 'not proven usable', does not omit the cross-tenant severity). Precise.

Section 8 OQ-5 filing: read decision 0014's OQ-5 text directly (docs/migration/decisions/0014-*.md lines 579-583) -- confirmed it names 'a BEAM scheduler itself blocked' as the literal concern, needing a load spike and S6 thresholds. Design's distinction between 'BEAM scheduler stall' (not observed, per its own scheduler_wall_time sampling) and 'native thread-pool exhaustion' (observed) is a real, substantively different mechanism, not hand-waving -- the former is a claim about BEAM's own schedulers, the latter about a separate native Tokio pool wasmex owns; confirmed the pool's separateness by reading engine.rs's TOKIO_RUNTIME definition directly.
Decision 0014 point (ii) exact text cross-checked at docs/migration/decisions/0014-*.md line 158/218 -- design's quotation is accurate.

Traceability table (section 10) checked against docs/requirements.yaml's REQ-170 entry (awk-extracted, not full-file read) -- all 7 real acceptance criteria present and correctly mapped, none omitted or invented.

Zero literal Elixir implementation code: grepped the design doc for defmodule/do-blocks/def/defp outside @spec/@type/@doc context -- only 'defmodule Letflow.Engine.Wasm.CallTimeout do' appears, immediately followed by @typedoc/@type/@doc/@spec declarations only (section 4.2), no function body anywhere. Section 4.3's code fences contain @spec lines only. PASS.
File placement / stray files: git status shows only this handoff as untracked; no stray files in project root.
result.skipped_verification: Deliberately did NOT re-run design section 1.5's 32-concurrent-hang saturation probe (the claim that 32 concurrent hangs starve an unrelated non-hanging guest call node-wide). Rationale: (1) the handoff explicitly authorized skipping it if judged unsafe/unnecessary; (2) it reportedly takes over a minute and durably occupies wasmex's shared, process-wide native Tokio thread pool for the remainder of any process that runs it -- re-running it in this validator's own process would leave this session (and any process tree it shares) with a degraded WASM pool for no incremental gate value; (3) the claim is not free-standing narrative -- it is fully corroborated by independent, cheaper evidence I *did* gather directly: reading store_executor.rs myself confirms the per-Store executor's JoinHandle is discarded and the executor task processes one command at a time to completion before dequeuing the next (an inherent, structural reason a stuck command blocks all subsequent commands on that Store, and by extension why a pool of N permanently-stuck worker threads == N invocations' worth of capacity gone from a fixed-size, node-global pool), and reading engine.rs confirms TOKIO_RUNTIME is a single process-wide LazyLock sized to available_parallelism(). Given the mechanism is independently confirmed at the source level and the qualitative claim (a fixed pool exhausted by N stuck threads eventually blocks unrelated work) follows directly and unavoidably from that mechanism, re-running the expensive 32-hang scenario would add confirmation of an arithmetic fact (32 > 8) rather than test a live-uncertain claim. This is stated explicitly per the handoff's own instruction, not silently omitted.
result.verdict: PASS -- no rework required. This is the most severe finding this pipeline has produced on the WASM half, and every load-bearing claim behind it withstood independent re-derivation from primary sources (my own live probes against real installed wasmex v0.15.1, and direct reading of wasmex's own Rust source, plugin_interface.ex, plugin_handler.ex, resource_limits.ex, decision 0014, and docs/requirements.yaml's REQ-170 entry). The design does not rubber-stamp decision 0014's claim, does not fabricate an interruption that doesn't occur, correctly identifies AC3 as needing zero new code (verified by direct reading, not trusted), specifies genuinely small and additive new code (CallTimeout module + a 3-line-shaped PluginHandler extension) with fully-specified signatures and error shapes, contains zero literal implementation code, and states the divergence plainly to ORCH/REVIEWER (section 7) and in the shipped moduledoc (section 6) rather than absorbing it. Traceability is complete against docs/requirements.yaml's real 7 acceptance criteria.
